learning_outcomes: translate a business goal into a conversion objective; model funnel and unit economics; define primary and guardrail metrics.
core_lesson: Conversion work starts with the business model, not a button colour. Define who pays, what is purchased, when value is realized, which costs vary with an order and what makes a customer valuable over time. Separate revenue from contribution and cash flow. A funnel is useful only when each stage has an operational definition and a denominator. Lead, qualified lead, opportunity, order and retained customer are not interchangeable. Choose a north-star outcome plus guardrails such as margin, refunds, cancellations, complaints and capacity.
workflow: (1) Map revenue model, customer, offer, pricing, fulfilment and repeat cycle. (2) Build a KPI tree from business outcome to journey behaviours and operational drivers. (3) Calculate baseline conversion and contribution using consistent population and period definitions. (4) List non-digital constraints such as stock, sales response, eligibility, pricing and delivery. (5) Write a conversion charter stating scope, owner, baseline, target, guardrails and exclusions.
practice: Use a synthetic subscription or commerce business. Model traffic, sessions, orders, AOV, gross margin, variable fulfilment cost, refund rate, paid acquisition cost and repeat behaviour. Compare a revenue-growth scenario with a contribution-growth scenario.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Business/conversion model and KPI tree. Show definitions, formulas, time window, source or synthetic label, assumptions, guardrails, capacity constraints and at least two scenarios. Reconcile subtotals and explain why a higher-revenue option may be rejected.

learning_outcomes: choose an appropriate research method; combine qualitative and quantitative evidence; distinguish observations, interpretations and hypotheses.
core_lesson: Research reduces decision uncertainty. Quantitative data shows the scale and distribution of behaviour; interviews and usability sessions help explain context, motivation and friction. Neither method proves more than its design permits. Recruitment must reflect the target population and task. Distinguish a customer statement, observed behaviour, analyst interpretation and business hypothesis. Triangulation means comparing independent evidence, not repeating the same assumption in three formats.
workflow: (1) Define the decision and research questions before choosing a method. (2) Specify segment, eligibility, recruitment, sample limitations and consent. (3) Collect behavioural analytics, support themes, reviews, surveys or interviews as appropriate. (4) Code evidence into needs, triggers, barriers and workarounds while preserving context. (5) Triangulate findings and label confidence, contradiction and unanswered questions.
practice: Investigate a synthetic checkout abandonment problem. Combine funnel data, five simulated interview transcripts and a usability observation log. Mark all material synthetic. Produce three insight statements with evidence links and competing explanations.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Research plan and evidence-backed insight report. Include research questions, method rationale, participant criteria, consent approach, sample caveats, evidence excerpts, coding scheme, contradictory evidence and prioritized opportunities.

learning_outcomes: specify reliable events and parameters; define identity and consent requirements; create implementation and QA controls.
core_lesson: Conversion analysis is only as trustworthy as its instrumentation. Start with the business question and event taxonomy, then define exposure, journey step, success and failure. Every event needs a trigger, parameters, owner, source, expected volume and validation rule. Distinguish event collection from identity resolution and attribution. Consent and privacy controls must be designed before data collection; technical ability to collect data does not establish permission to collect it.
workflow: (1) Translate decisions into metrics and an event dictionary. (2) Map page/screen, action, trigger, event name, parameters and allowed values. (3) Specify identity, consent state, retention, access and suppression. (4) Define implementation owner, environment, test data and expected sequence. (5) Test duplicate, missing, malformed, out-of-order and consent-denied cases; record release criteria.
practice: Create a measurement specification for a three-step application form. Include view, start, validation error, step completion, submit and confirmed outcome. Test duplicate submit and consent denied.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Measurement specification and analytics QA checklist. Include event names, triggers, parameters, data types, sample payloads, consent handling, identity assumptions, source of truth, test cases, owners and known limitations.

learning_outcomes: diagnose funnel leakage by segment; quantify opportunity; distinguish measurement defects from genuine user friction.
core_lesson: A funnel is a sequence of explicitly defined eligible events. Conversion between adjacent stages is not interchangeable with end-to-end conversion. Segment comparisons require stable definitions, adequate sample and attention to selection effects. A large drop-off is not automatically an opportunity: it may be an expected choice, eligibility filter, instrumentation gap or duplicate event. Begin with data quality and cohort construction, then size the opportunity under realistic constraints.
workflow: (1) Validate event sequence, deduplication, timezone, eligibility and population definitions. (2) Calculate step conversion, abandonment and end-to-end rate with denominators. (3) Segment by device, source, audience, product and relevant context. (4) Quantify affected volume and plausible recoverable share without assuming every exit is fixable. (5) Rank issues by evidence, impact, confidence, effort and risk.
practice: Analyze a synthetic five-step funnel with device and traffic-source splits. Introduce one tracking defect and one genuine UX issue; distinguish them through reconciliation checks.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Funnel diagnosis and quantified opportunity backlog. Include metric definitions, baseline, segment sample sizes, data-quality checks, opportunity formulas, confidence, alternative explanations and owners.

learning_outcomes: evaluate usability and information architecture; identify accessibility and journey barriers; prioritize evidence-backed improvements.
core_lesson: UX optimization helps a person complete a task accurately and confidently. Inspect information scent, navigation, content hierarchy, mobile behaviour, form labels, error recovery, trust cues, loading, accessibility and post-submit confirmation. Heuristics identify candidate issues but do not prove impact. Heatmaps and session replays supply behavioural clues, not representative explanations of every user. Pair observation with task success and customer research.
workflow: (1) Define target user, task, context and success criteria. (2) Audit supported devices, keyboard paths and error states. (3) Inspect analytics, user feedback, usability evidence and privacy-safe behaviour tools. (4) Describe each issue by user, context, evidence, severity and task impact. (5) Prioritize fixes and specify post-release verification.
practice: Audit a synthetic mobile product-detail-to-checkout journey. Record five issues, distinguish accessibility blockers from preference issues, and prototype two improvements.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: UX/CX audit with prioritized recommendations. Each issue includes screenshot or reproducible description, affected task, evidence, severity rationale, accessibility/privacy consideration, recommended change and verification metric.

learning_outcomes: translate evidence into falsifiable hypotheses; estimate potential value; prioritize opportunities with explicit confidence, effort and risk.
core_lesson: A hypothesis states a change, target population, expected mechanism and measurable outcome. It is not a feature request disguised as a sentence. ICE or impact-confidence-effort scores are discussion aids, not objective truth; anchors and evidence must be visible. Estimate value with ranges and distinguish potential gross uplift from net incremental contribution. Include dependencies, customer harm, implementation risk and opportunity cost.
workflow: (1) Write the observed problem and evidence before proposing a solution. (2) State intervention, audience, mechanism, primary metric and guardrails. (3) Estimate eligible population, baseline and realistic effect range. (4) Score impact, confidence, effort, dependencies and risk using defined anchors. (5) Create a ranked backlog and document why lower-ranked ideas were deferred.
practice: Turn eight observed checkout or onboarding issues into hypotheses. Prioritize them under a fixed engineering capacity constraint and show how ranking changes under a risk-first scenario.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Ranked experiment backlog with traceable evidence, hypothesis statements, metric definitions, value range, confidence rationale, effort/dependency, risk, owner and decision status.

learning_outcomes: choose a valid test design; define treatment, assignment and exposure; pre-specify metrics, guardrails and decision rules.
core_lesson: An experiment compares outcomes under a planned assignment mechanism. A/B randomization supports causal inference only when assignment, exposure, measurement and analysis assumptions hold. Define the randomization unit, eligibility, allocation, treatment, contamination risk, duration rationale and stopping rule. The primary metric must reflect the decision; guardrails detect harm. Pre-register analysis and avoid changing success criteria after seeing results.
workflow: (1) Translate the hypothesis into treatment/control and define randomization unit. (2) Specify eligibility, exclusions, assignment, exposure logging and crossover rules. (3) Choose one primary metric plus diagnostic and guardrail metrics. (4) Estimate sample requirement and duration from baseline, minimum detectable effect, alpha, power and traffic. (5) Pre-register analysis, stopping, decision and rollout conditions; QA before exposure.
practice: Design an A/B test for a checkout progress indicator. Specify assignment, exposure event, primary conversion, revenue/margin guardrails, sample-size assumptions, duration constraint and stop conditions.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Experiment brief and pre-registration plan. It must be implementable by product, engineering and analytics without undocumented decisions; include randomization, event QA, analysis, risk and rollback.

learning_outcomes: interpret sample size and power; distinguish statistical from practical significance; identify multiplicity, peeking and validity problems.
core_lesson: Statistical significance is not business importance. Define the estimand, unit, baseline, effect scale, uncertainty interval, alpha, power and minimum detectable effect. For binary conversion, a planning approximation depends on baseline rate, detectable difference, alpha and power; final methods must account for variance, clustering, repeated observations and platform design. Repeated peeking, unplanned comparisons and post-hoc subgroup hunting can inflate false positives.
workflow: (1) State target effect in absolute and relative terms. (2) Estimate sample size with a documented method and defensible baseline. (3) Check randomization, sample-ratio mismatch, novelty, seasonality, interference and tracking. (4) Report effect estimate, interval and practical interpretation. (5) Account for multiplicity and stopping design; document inconclusive outcomes.
practice: Analyze synthetic binary-conversion and revenue-per-user experiments. Compare effect size, interval width, power assumptions and commercial value; include an inconclusive result.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Statistical analysis report with assumptions, sample-size method, data checks, effect estimates, uncertainty intervals, multiplicity handling, decision and limitations.

learning_outcomes: specify implementation; validate assignment and exposure; test events, rendering, performance, privacy and rollback.
core_lesson: A sound design can fail because the experience renders incorrectly, variants leak, assignment changes across sessions or events fire twice. Technical QA covers configuration, targeting, bucketing, exposure, event collection, cross-browser behaviour, performance, accessibility, consent and rollback. Separate implementation correctness from outcome analysis. A test must not launch simply because an editor preview looks right.
workflow: (1) Translate the brief into configuration, code and data contracts. (2) Validate targeting, persistent assignment, rendering and fallback. (3) Test events, deduplication, exposure and analytics reconciliation. (4) Check device/browser, performance, accessibility and consent behaviour. (5) Define staged rollout, monitoring, rollback owner and post-launch verification.
practice: Create an implementation and QA plan for a form-layout experiment, including logged-in/out users, devices, consent denial, cached pages and a rollback failure scenario.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Implementation plan and test QA log with test matrix, expected/actual output, severity, evidence, owner, fix verification and go/no-go recommendation.

learning_outcomes: select a credible causal design; distinguish attribution from incrementality; communicate assumptions and generalizability.
core_lesson: Attribution assigns credit according to a rule; incrementality estimates what would not have happened without the intervention. A randomized holdout is often strong when feasible, but customer randomization may be unsuitable because of spillover, shared devices, marketplace effects or operational constraints. Geo tests and matched-market designs require comparable regions, sufficient pre-periods and stable boundaries. Difference-in-differences depends on a defensible parallel-trends assumption. Report uncertainty and limits.
workflow: (1) Define causal question, treatment, outcome, population and horizon. (2) Choose design based on randomization feasibility, spillover and available units. (3) Set baseline/pre-period, comparison group and contamination controls. (4) Predefine estimator, uncertainty and sensitivity checks. (5) Interpret causal estimate separately from attributed conversions and platform-reported credit.
practice: Compare a user-level holdout and geo experiment for a fictional regional promotion. Identify where spillover, low volume and pre-trend differences weaken the alternatives.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Incrementality plan with design rationale, unit, assignment, pre-period, outcome, assumptions, analysis method, sample/region criteria, risks and limitations.

learning_outcomes: design eligible audience rules; document data provenance and consent; measure personalization with safeguards.
core_lesson: Personalization is a decision system, not the insertion of a first name. Start with a user need or journey context, then decide whether a different experience plausibly improves the outcome. Document data provenance, eligibility, freshness, suppression, frequency, channel conflicts and user control. Avoid sensitive inference and unfair proxies. A personalized experience needs a baseline comparison and a clear exit when data is missing or stale.
workflow: (1) Identify a journey need and define audience rule. (2) Document data source, freshness, purpose, consent, exclusions and access. (3) Design content/offer variants with fallback and frequency policy. (4) Coordinate channel timing, suppression and preference management. (5) Measure incremental journey outcome and monitor complaints, fairness and fatigue.
practice: Design a post-signup onboarding journey for new and returning customers. Include data minimization, fallback content, contact caps and an experiment plan.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Personalization strategy and measurement plan with audience definitions, data map, consent/purpose, decision rules, variant rationale, fallback, frequency, suppression, KPIs and risk controls.

learning_outcomes: establish an experimentation operating model; govern intake and capacity; preserve reusable organizational learning.
core_lesson: A mature programme is measured by decision quality and learning, not test count. Governance defines intake, evidence thresholds, prioritization, capacity, design review, QA, launch permissions, analysis ownership, knowledge retention and escalation. Portfolio management balances foundational fixes, high-risk tests and strategic bets. Every experiment needs a decision owner and path for shipping, iterating or stopping. Preserve negative and inconclusive results.
workflow: (1) Set programme charter, scope, decision rights and critical-failure rules. (2) Create intake and triage with readiness requirements. (3) Allocate engineering, design, analytics and research capacity. (4) Run design/statistical/technical review before launch and analysis review after completion. (5) Maintain searchable repository, decision log and quarterly learning review.
practice: Create a quarterly operating model for a product team with one engineer, one analyst and limited design support. Allocate capacity and show escalation for a privacy-critical issue.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: CRO programme operating model with RACI, stages, templates, capacity model, risk gates, review cadence, repository fields, learning KPIs and executive reporting.

learning_outcomes: translate results into defensible financial impact; compare investment alternatives; present an accountable executive decision.
core_lesson: Executives need a decision, not a chart gallery. Convert tested effects into expected contribution using eligible population, adoption, persistence, unit economics and implementation cost. Separate observed results from forecast rollout value. Show uncertainty and downside risk; do not extrapolate a short test into a full-year result without assumptions. A recommendation includes no-change and alternative options, dependencies, implementation owner and a post-launch verification plan.
workflow: (1) Summarize decision, evidence, population and result. (2) Translate effect into a financial model with explicit scenario assumptions. (3) Subtract implementation, operational and variable costs; show sensitivity. (4) Compare alternatives, downside, opportunity cost and risks. (5) Write executive recommendation with owner, timing, guardrails and review date.
practice: Prepare a two-page investment memo for a checkout improvement with uncertain conversion lift and measurable implementation cost.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Executive business case and recommendation narrative. Show base/upside/downside, net contribution, time horizon, evidence versus forecast, risks, alternatives and decision requested.

learning_outcomes: integrate research, analytics, UX, experimentation and leadership; defend technical and causal validity; present a commercial roadmap.
core_lesson: The capstone demonstrates a complete chain from business problem to sustained outcome. A polished presentation cannot compensate for invalid measurement or unsupported claims. Show how a research signal becomes an opportunity, why the intervention was selected, how it was implemented and tested, what the result means, and what leadership should do next. Use synthetic evidence where live access is unavailable and label it throughout. Recommendations must respect capacity, privacy and uncertainty.
workflow: (1) Frame business problem, audience, value model and journey scope. (2) Synthesize research, analytics and UX evidence into a prioritized opportunity set. (3) Design and technically QA one experiment plus an appropriate measurement alternative. (4) Analyze results, uncertainty, guardrails and commercial implications. (5) Present a 90-day roadmap, governance model and executive decision request.
practice: Build an end-to-end CRO portfolio for a fictional Indonesian commerce or subscription product. Include one completed synthetic experiment and one future test with a defensible causal plan.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: CRO strategy and portfolio presentation plus evidence workbook. Include business model, research, journey audit, KPI/event map, opportunity backlog, experiment brief, QA record, results/uncertainty, financial case, governance and 90-day roadmap.

learning_outcomes: map the parties in an offline media transaction; explain planning, buying, delivery and reconciliation responsibilities; identify conflicts of interest and decision rights.
core_lesson: Offline media is an ecosystem of advertisers, agencies, media owners, sales houses, measurement providers, production suppliers, verification partners and specialist vendors. The same organization may perform more than one role, so the learner must identify who owns inventory, who sells it, who measures audience, who validates delivery and who approves payment. An agency workflow connects brief intake, research, strategy, plan, proposal, negotiation, booking, material delivery, campaign monitoring, post-buy and invoice reconciliation. Clear accountability prevents gaps between what was promised, bought, delivered and billed.
workflow: (1) Identify advertiser, agency, media owner, measurement provider and third-party suppliers. (2) Map each party's commercial interest, data access and accountability. (3) Draw the campaign workflow and approval gates. (4) Assign RACI for budget, schedule, creative, legal, delivery, reporting and payment. (5) Document conflict checks, escalation path and records retention.
practice: Build an ecosystem map and RACI for a fictional national consumer campaign involving a TV broadcaster, radio network, OOH operator, agency and audience-measurement supplier.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Ecosystem map and campaign workflow. Include all stakeholders, money/inventory/data flows, owners, approvals, handoffs, conflicts and escalation. Every key activity must have one accountable owner.

learning_outcomes: translate a business audience into a media target; assess research quality and representativeness; document gaps between target audience and measured universe.
core_lesson: Audience research begins with the commercial question: whom must the campaign influence, in what geography and purchase context, and what behaviour matters? Demographic descriptions alone often conceal differences in need, category use, media habits, language, affordability and decision authority. Research may combine survey, panel, census, customer data, location data and qualitative insight. Every source has a universe, fieldwork period, sample frame, weighting, question wording and limitation. Do not combine incomparable sources as if they measure the same population.
workflow: (1) Define the target audience and buying/usage behaviour. (2) Specify geography, age or other permitted characteristics, category and time period. (3) Inventory research sources and inspect universe, sample, fieldwork, weighting and method. (4) Identify coverage gaps, duplication and confidence limitations. (5) Translate evidence into a media audience brief and supplier questions.
practice: Compare three fictional audience sources for an Indonesian personal-care category: a syndicated panel, a client CRM extract and a qualitative study. Identify what each can and cannot support.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Audience intelligence report with audience definition, need-state/context, geography, source metadata, methodology, sample limitations, media behaviours, contradictions and planning implications.

learning_outcomes: interpret reach, frequency, ratings, GRP/TRP and media-specific metrics; inspect measurement methodology; avoid invalid aggregation across currencies.
core_lesson: Rating points, reach and frequency are related but not interchangeable. For a defined target and measurement period, GRP is commonly expressed as reach percentage multiplied by average frequency; a rating is an audience percentage under a specified universe and unit. Reach is the share or count exposed at least once; frequency describes repeated exposure among reached units. Print circulation is copies distributed under a defined audit, while readership estimates people reading or accessing a publication. OOH methodologies estimate opportunity or likelihood of exposure using location, visibility and movement assumptions. The unit, universe, period and method are essential to interpretation.
workflow: (1) Read the measurement definition and target universe. (2) Verify period, geography, unit, sample and collection method. (3) Calculate or interpret rating, reach, frequency, GRP/TRP, CPM and CPP only with consistent bases. (4) Inspect duplication, co-viewing, panel error, modeled values and audit status. (5) State what comparisons are valid and what cannot be added or converted.
practice: Use a synthetic TV schedule and two competing audience reports. Calculate GRP and CPP; identify a reach-duplication problem and explain why adding station reach percentages overstates total campaign reach.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Measurement evaluation with formula sheet, universe, source/method metadata, calculation checks, duplication caveat, confidence limitation and a written recommendation about whether the sources are comparable.

learning_outcomes: construct a TV/broadcast schedule; evaluate audience composition, reach, frequency and cost; account for inventory and delivery constraints.
core_lesson: TV planning balances target audience, programme context, daypart, spot length, schedule weight, reach, frequency, cost and creative suitability. A low-cost spot may deliver little target audience or cluster exposure inefficiently. A schedule must specify station, programme/daypart, date, position, duration, spot count, rating assumption, gross and net cost, audience target and cancellation conditions. Ratings are estimates under a defined measurement system; campaign reach and duplication require a valid cross-programme or cross-channel method. Do not convert a platform forecast into a guarantee.
workflow: (1) Confirm brief, target, geography, dates, objective and budget. (2) Compare station/programme inventory, audience profile and quality. (3) Build alternative schedules and calculate rating points, reach/frequency where supported, CPM/CPP and cost. (4) Apply placement, separation, adjacency and brand-safety rules. (5) Record assumptions, booking deadlines, material specs and reconciliation method.
practice: Prepare two schedules for a fictional consumer launch: one reach-led and one frequency-led. Use simulated ratings and net rates; label all assumptions and test a 10% inventory shortfall.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: TV plan and schedule rationale with target definition, inventory, placement, ratings, GRP, reach/frequency method, cost, schedule weight, creative requirements, exclusions and sensitivity scenario.

learning_outcomes: compare broadcast, streaming and other audio environments; build a spot or audio schedule; evaluate cost and audience fit.
core_lesson: Audio includes terrestrial radio, digital radio, streaming, podcasts and other sound-led environments. These channels differ in audience measurement, buying unit, ad insertion, targeting, reporting and creative context. Radio planning may use station audience, daypart, programme, spot length and frequency; digital audio may use impressions, completed listens or platform-defined actions. Do not equate a broadcast audience estimate with a digital ad-server impression. Creative quality, repetition, language, local relevance and sound environment influence delivery and response.
workflow: (1) Define audience, geography, occasion and role of audio. (2) Compare station, programme, podcast or streaming inventory and measurement currency. (3) Build spot/ad schedule with daypart, length, frequency and budget. (4) Confirm creative production, copy approval, trafficking and proof. (5) Reconcile planned versus delivered spots/listens and evaluate outcomes.
practice: Build a four-week audio plan for a local retail launch with radio and podcast options. Use simulated audience/cost data and separate broadcast reach from digital impression estimates.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Radio/audio plan with audience rationale, inventory, schedule, spot length, reach/frequency basis, cost, creative spec, measurement definition, delivery proof and evaluation plan.

learning_outcomes: evaluate publication audience and circulation evidence; select format and placement; compare print proposals and delivery terms.
core_lesson: Print investment depends on publication audience, editorial context, issue frequency, format, position, geography, circulation and readership methodology. Circulation is not identical to unique readers. A copy may be shared, remain unread or reach a different audience than the campaign's intended target. Compare audited circulation, readership research and publisher claims on their own definitions. Placement premiums, insertions, advertorials, supplements and production costs must be separated from media cost. Editorial association and disclosure rules require review.
workflow: (1) Define target, geography, issue date and communication role. (2) Evaluate publications, editorial context and audience evidence. (3) Compare circulation/readership definition, audit, period and duplication. (4) Select size, position, format, insertion and creative production. (5) Specify material deadline, proof of publication, cancellation and billing terms.
practice: Compare three fictional publication proposals for a financial-services campaign. Detect an apples-to-oranges comparison where one supplier presents circulation, another readership and another claimed monthly visitors.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Print recommendation and placement plan with source definitions, audience fit, issue schedule, circulation/readership limitations, format, net rates, production fees, disclosure requirements and proof-of-publication.

learning_outcomes: evaluate OOH/DOOH sites and formats; distinguish traffic, opportunity-to-see and modeled exposure; plan coverage and delivery verification.
core_lesson: Out-of-home investment is location- and context-dependent. A site evaluation considers audience flow, direction, dwell time, line of sight, obstruction, illumination, operating hours, environment, creative legibility and proximity to a relevant occasion. DOOH adds screen loops, share of voice, proof-of-play and dynamic scheduling. Traffic counts are not automatically people exposed; opportunity-to-see is not equivalent to a verified individual impression. Exposure methodology must state data source, mobility assumptions, visibility, duplication and limitations. Location-level reach should not be summed without a defensible deduplication method.
workflow: (1) Define target geography, audience movement and campaign occasion. (2) Map sites, formats, visibility, dwell and inventory availability. (3) Review audience/exposure methodology, source period and model. (4) Build location/format mix, schedule, share of voice and budget. (5) Specify proof-of-play, photographs, uptime, maintenance, makegoods and post-campaign validation.
practice: Evaluate ten fictional Jakarta OOH/DOOH sites for a retail opening. Use synthetic traffic and visibility data; identify sites with high traffic but poor target or viewing conditions.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: OOH/DOOH plan with location map, format, audience rationale, exposure method, time/loop assumptions, cost, creative spec, proof requirements and limitations.

learning_outcomes: evaluate cinema and partnership inventory; value rights and deliverables; establish measurement and contract controls.
core_lesson: Cinema and sponsorship combine audience access with context, association and experience. They may include screen ads, foyer placements, product sampling, event integration, naming rights, category exclusivity, content rights, hospitality and data capture. The proposal should distinguish guaranteed deliverables from estimated exposure, editorial association and optional value-add. A sponsorship valuation is not a simple media-equivalent multiplier; it must explain audience relevance, rights, activation cost, exclusivity, duration, usage rights and evidence of delivery.
workflow: (1) Define objective and desired audience experience. (2) Inventory rights, placements, access, exclusivity and activation options. (3) Value each deliverable using cost, audience, quality and strategic fit. (4) Review production, approvals, safety, data collection, talent and usage rights. (5) Set proof, reporting, cancellation, replacement and makegood terms.
practice: Evaluate a fictional cinema-and-festival package. Separate guaranteed screen spots, estimated attendance, sampling rights, data capture, category exclusivity and optional social posts.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Partnership proposal and valuation framework with rights matrix, deliverables, value assumptions, activation cost, audience evidence, usage/term limits, measurement, risks and negotiation conditions.

learning_outcomes: allocate offline budget across channels; compare scenarios and marginal returns; handle audience duplication and measurement limits.
core_lesson: Media mix connects target, communication role, schedule, budget and measurement. Reach, frequency, context and cost are not directly comparable across channels without a defined framework. A plan should show why each channel is included, which audience or occasion it contributes, and what trade-off it creates. Use scenarios rather than a single unexplained allocation. Optimize toward the business objective while respecting minimum commitments, inventory, creative supply, geographic coverage and measurement uncertainty. Do not sum cross-media reach without a compatible deduplication method.
workflow: (1) Set objective, target, geography, timing and constraints. (2) Assign roles to TV, audio, print, OOH, cinema and partnerships. (3) Build low/base/high investment scenarios with explicit assumptions. (4) Examine reach, frequency, duplication, marginal cost and channel complementarity. (5) Define reallocation triggers and guardrails.
practice: Allocate a fixed synthetic budget across TV, audio, OOH and print for a regional product launch. Create two alternatives and show how the plan changes if TV inventory becomes unavailable.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Integrated media flowchart and allocation rationale with budget reconciliation, audience role, reach/frequency basis, assumptions, duplication caveat, marginal trade-offs, inventory dependency and scenario triggers.

learning_outcomes: evaluate rate cards and proposals; prepare negotiation objectives and BATNA; document commercial terms and risk.
core_lesson: A rate card is an asking price, not proof of value or a complete offer. Compare net rates, audience, inventory, position, timing, production, fees, data, exclusivity, value-add, cancellation, payment, proof and makegood terms. Negotiation begins with the advertiser's objective, target, walk-away point, alternatives and approval authority. Concessions should be exchanged deliberately and valued at expected use, not nominal list price. Legal terms, tax, currency, liability, brand safety and cancellation must be escalated to authorized reviewers.
workflow: (1) Build comparable proposals with normalized units and costs. (2) Define target outcome, BATNA, reservation point and tradeable concessions. (3) Prioritize price, quality, added value, inventory, data and flexibility. (4) Record every concession, approval and contractual condition. (5) Reconcile signed terms against booking and invoice.
practice: Run a negotiation simulation between agency and publisher for a campaign with fixed dates and budget. Evaluate an offer containing a discount, bonus spots, a premium placement and a makegood clause.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Negotiation plan and commercial evaluation with apples-to-apples comparison, BATNA, target/limit, concession strategy, fee/tax treatment, risk, approval, agreed terms and post-negotiation summary.

learning_outcomes: translate an approved plan into accurate bookings; manage material and approval dependencies; maintain a complete audit trail.
core_lesson: Buying operations turns strategy into enforceable instructions. The booking must match the approved budget, media plan, owner, inventory, dates, format, audience, pricing and terms. Creative delivery has technical and legal dependencies: duration, aspect, file format, audio level, copy approval, sponsorship integration, proof and deadline. Changes must be versioned and approved; informal email changes can create a dispute between booked and delivered activity. A buying pack should let another operator execute the campaign without verbal context.
workflow: (1) Reconcile approved plan and budget authority. (2) Issue or verify insertion order/booking confirmation and all terms. (3) Collect creative specification, asset, clearance and approval. (4) Confirm schedule, material receipt, trafficking and escalation contacts. (5) Maintain change log and daily/weekly delivery checks.
practice: Prepare a buying documentation pack for a mixed TV, radio and OOH campaign. Inject a late creative replacement and a site outage; show change control.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Booking pack and execution checklist with approved plan, PO/IO, dates, cost, spec, materials, clearance, contacts, RACI, changes, delivery evidence and escalation path.

learning_outcomes: reconcile planned, contracted, delivered and billed activity; assess proof; resolve shortfalls and makegoods.
core_lesson: Post-buy compares plan, booking, actual delivery, measurement and invoice. Each number must retain its source and definition. A missing spot, incorrect date, poor placement, screen downtime or audience underdelivery is not the same issue and needs different evidence. Makegood, credit or refund depends on contract terms, tolerance, deadlines and proof. A good post-buy does not hide shortfall inside a blended average; it identifies root cause, financial exposure and the remedy agreed with the owner.
workflow: (1) Collect approved plan, signed booking and delivery logs. (2) Obtain proof-of-airing, proof-of-publication, proof-of-play, photos or relevant third-party measurement. (3) Reconcile booked versus delivered by line item. (4) Calculate under/over delivery and invoice variance using contractual rules. (5) Agree remedy, owner, deadline and closure evidence; capture next-cycle learning.
practice: A synthetic DOOH buy has 12% underdelivery across three locations and a TV spot aired in the wrong daypart. Calculate the disputed delivery and propose remedies under a stated mock contract.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Post-buy report and reconciliation log with line-level planned/booked/delivered/billed values, evidence links, variance, root cause, contract clause, remedy, approval and closure.

learning_outcomes: establish comparable measurement principles; create auditability and controls; govern conflicts, data and investment risk.
core_lesson: Governance protects the integrity of investment decisions. A measurement scorecard should distinguish delivery, audience, quality, brand outcome and business outcome. Cross-media reach requires compatible universes, time periods and deduplication; otherwise present separate channel measures and explain the gap. Procurement controls cover authorization, conflicts, rebates or value-add disclosure, supplier selection, contract storage, invoice verification and records retention. Third-party measurement can improve assurance but is not automatically error-free or available for every market and format.
workflow: (1) Define governance objectives, decision rights and measurement scope. (2) Create metric dictionary and source hierarchy. (3) Design procurement, conflict disclosure, approval and invoice controls. (4) Require evidence and exception handling for each major investment. (5) Review supplier performance, data access, audit findings and corrective action.
practice: Design a governance framework for a fictional annual media investment with multiple agencies and suppliers. Include a conflict declaration, approval matrix, evidence hierarchy and exception log.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Governance framework and measurement scorecard with metric definitions, source hierarchy, audit trail, approval limits, conflicts, supplier scorecard, invoice checks, privacy, retention and escalation.

learning_outcomes: lead an integrated offline investment recommendation; defend commercial and measurement assumptions; present delivery and governance accountability.
core_lesson: The senior capstone tests the entire investment chain from client brief to post-buy. It must show why each channel is selected, what role it plays, how audience evidence supports the decision, how the plan is bought and delivered, and how the investment will be reconciled. Leadership requires more than a schedule: it requires commercial judgment, supplier management, team design, scenario planning, escalation, transparency and client communication. All simulated data must be labelled; local audience and trading claims require current source evidence.
workflow: (1) Frame business objective, target, geography, budget and risk. (2) Build audience evidence and channel strategy. (3) Produce TV/audio/print/OOH/cinema scenarios and a commercial comparison. (4) Create booking, delivery, governance and post-buy controls. (5) Present the investment decision, uncertainty, trade-offs and 90-day operating plan.
practice: Build a senior integrated offline plan for a fictional consumer brand launching in five Indonesian cities. Include a national and local mix, a fixed budget, a supplier conflict scenario and a 10% delivery shortfall scenario.
required_artifact_and_acceptance: Senior investment plan and client presentation plus workbook. Include brief, target, source methodology, channel roles, schedules, budget, negotiated terms, buying pack, delivery evidence model, measurement scorecard, risk/governance, post-buy and executive recommendation.
